own_scenes.family: Otras escenas: Filadelfia, el Medio Oeste, Virginia
own_scenes.desc: Antes de N.W.A, el gangster rap nació en Filadelfia: Schoolly D, con DJ Code Money al scratch y una Roland 909 tocada en directo, grabó en una noche de porros «P.S.K. What Does It Mean?», homenaje a la banda Parkside Killers, y «Gucci Time» (1985): armas, sexo, drogas, una de las primeras veces que sonó «nigga» en un disco y litros de reverberación, «un sonido de polvo de ángel». Chris Schwartz, luego cofundador de Ruffhouse, fue su mánager y sello; Lady B, la madrina de la radio de Filadelfia, le pidió quitar los tacos y acabó editando ella la cinta. Le contrataban clubes de rock blancos. Para Lady B, «el gangster rapero original». Él distingue el gangster rap, celebrar una elección personal, del gangsta rap, celebrar la vida del barrio; se cansó de explicar a la prensa que su protagonista no aprieta el gatillo.

refs.q: That’s the first gangster rapper. Not N.W.A, not anybody on the West Coast. That is the original gangster rapper right there.
refs.para: It just felt like to me that the Philadelphia hip-hop community just felt proud of him and rocked with him, and what he’s saying is really just how we talk every day on the corner, but he put it on the record. That’s the first gangster rapper. Not N.W.A, not anybody on the West Coast. That is the original gangster rapper right there.

refs.q: My reaction was, you wouldn’t tell Picasso to change his art.
refs.para: Schoolly D (artist, Philadelphia): My reaction was, you wouldn’t tell Picasso to change his art. People are so afraid of art and what it can change. They want you to just fall in line. I was like, Well, who the fuck is gonna tell our story then, if I’m not gonna do it?

refs.q: There’s gangster rap and gangsta rap.
refs.para: Schoolly D (artist, Philadelphia): There’s gangster rap and gangsta rap. Gangster rap is a celebration of a personal choice. You can be a preacher and do something gangster. You can be a mother…Mom’s gangster. That means Mom ain’t taking no shit. That’s gangster rap, e-r.

podcast.title: Characterized by Delinquent Imagery and Themes
podcast.body: Rapers in this subgenre were often depicted with gold chains, portraying a delinquent image, discussing shootings, women, aggression, prison, and originating from suburbs. This prototype of rap became deeply ingrained in public perception. "Los raperos van con cadenas de oro, son delincuente, se hablan de tiros, de tías buenas, son agresivos, es entranza de la cárcel, tienen todos estos problemas, vienen de suburbios, este prototipo un poco del rap que todos tenemos tan asentado."

srcs.episode: Poniendo a Kanye West en su lugar

podcast.title: Dominant in the 1990s
podcast.body: Gangster rap absolutely dominated the hip hop scene from the mid-1990s, becoming the "great era" of mainstream hip hop. This period brought forth major artists but also became somewhat "caricature-like" by the late 1990s, leading to a sense of exhaustion. "El rap y del hip hop de mitad de los 90, la verdad es que la época de mitad de los 90 del hip hop es una etapa un poco curiosa porque está absolutamente dominada por lo que entendemos por el gangster rap."

podcast.title: Hip Hop Generation Gap
podcast.body: Gangster rap fans are identified as part of the "old schoolers" within hip hop, who are now "pitted against the Drake's and Chris Browns of today," highlighting a generational divide in the genre.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Late 90s/Early 2000s Decline and Evolution
podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, after many years of prominence, gangster rap began to feel "relatively exhausted" and almost "caricature-like." Artists like 50 Cent and Jay-Z, while important, represented a late evolution of this style, maintaining the "almost delinquent" image with weapons and aggressive themes, although some, like Eminem, had more "evolutive" lyrics. "Empieza a estar relativamente agotado y empieza a ser un poco casi caricaturezco y cuando ya nos vamos hacia finales de los 90 que ya tenemos a 50 cent, tenemos a J7, tenemos a muchos otros artistas muy importantes, siguen siendo una evolución un poco tardía de lo que viene a ser esos restos en el gangster rap."

podcast.title: Part of 1990s Musical Diversity
podcast.body: Gangster rap was a significant element within the broad musical changes observed between 1991 and 1995. This era was characterized by a rapid emergence of diverse genres and scenes. "the entire Lola Paloose generation was gangster rap."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise and Fragmentation of Music Video Culture
podcast.body: The rise of gangster rap contributed significantly to the fragmentation of music video culture. Alongside alt-rock, it helped divide everything into distinct "scenes," leading to the demise of the music video monoculture and prompting video channels to develop genre-specific programming like "Yo MTV Raps" and "Raps City." "Together with the rise of hip-hop, especially gangster rap, everything was divided into scenes."
